source_text: Aeque stationes nostras, ut indignas; quasdam vero et in serum constitutas, novitatis nomine incusant, hoc quoque munus et ex arbitrio obeundum esse dicentes, et non ultra nonam detinendum, de suo scilicet more. Sed quod pertineat ad interdictionis quaestionem, semel pro omnibus caussis respondebo. Nunc ad proprium hujus speciei articulum, de modo temporis dico, de ipsis prius expostulandum, unde hanc formam nova dirimendis stationibus praescribant. Si, quia Petrus, et qui cum eo, ad horam nonam orationis templum introgressi leguntur, quis mihi probabit illos ea die statione functos, ut horam nonam ad clausulam et expunctionem stationis interpretetur? Atqui facilius invenias Petrum hora sexta capiendi cibi caussa, prius in superiora ad orandum ascendisse, quo magis sexta diei finiri officio huic possit, quae illud absolutura post orationem videbatur. Porro, cum in eodem commentario Lucae, et tertia hora orationis demonstretur, sub qua Spiritu Sancto initiati, pro ebriis habebantur; et sexta, qua Petrus ascendit in superiora; et nona, qua templum sunt introgressi, cur non intelligamus salva plane indifferentia semper et ubique et omni tempore orandi, tamen tres istas horas ut insigniores in rebus humanis, quae diem distribuunt, quae negotia distinguunt, quae publice resonant, ita et solemniores fuisse in orationibus divinis? Quod etiam suadet Danielis quoque argumentum ter die orantis, utique per aliquarum horarum exceptionem, non aliarum autem quam insigniorum, exinde Apostolicorum, tertiae, sextae, nonae. Hinc itaque et Petrum dicam ex vetere potius usu nonam observasse, tertio orantem supremae orationis munere. Haec autem propter illos, qui se putant ex forma Petri agere, quam ignorant; non quasi respuamus nonam, cui et quarta sabbati, et sexta plurimum fungimur: sed quia eorum quae ex traditione observantur, tanto magis dignam rationem afferre debemus, quanto carent Scripturae auctoritate, donec aliquo coelesti charismate aut confirmentur, aut corrigantur. Et si qua, inquit, ignoratis, Dominus vobis revelabit. Itaque, seposito confirmatore omnium istorum Paracleto, duce universae veritatis, an indignior apud vos ratio afferatur in nonam observandi requiro, ut etiam Petro ea ratio deputanda sit, si statione tunc functus est. Venit enim de exitu Domini, quem etsi semper commemorari oportet sine differentia horarum, impressius tamen tum ei secundum ipsum stationis vocabulum addicimur: nam et milites nunquam immemores sacramenti, magis stationibus parent. Itaque in eam usque horam celebranda pressura est, in qua a sexta contenebratus orbis defuncto domino lugubre fecit officium, ut tunc et nos revertamur ad jucunditatem, cum et mundus recepit claritatem. Hoc si magis ad religionem sapit christianam, dum magis Christi gloriam celebrat, possum aeque serae stationis ex eodem rei ordine statum figere, ut jejunemus ad serum, exspectantes tempus Dominicae sepulturae cum Joseph postulatum detulit corpus, et condidit. Inde et irreligiosum est ante famulorum carnem refrigerare, quam domini. Sed hoc ex argumentationum provocatione commiserim, conjecturas conjecturis, et tamen puto fidelioribus, repercutiens. Videamus an aliquid tale nobis de vetustatibus quoque patrocinetur. In Exodo, habitus ille Moysis adversus Amalech orationibus praeliantis usque in occasum perseverans, nonne statio fuit sera? Jesum Nave debellantem Amorrhaeos, prandisse illa die existimamus, qua ipsis elementis stationem imperavit? Stetit sol in Gabaon, et luna in Aialon: stetit sol et luna instructione, donec ultus est populus de inimicis suis; et stetit sol medio coelo, et non accedebat in occasum, et in finem diei unius. Non fuit dies talis retro et in novissimo, utique tam prolixus; ut, inquit, exaudiret Deus hominem, parem scilicet solis, instantem tamdiu in officio, stationem etiam sera longiorem. Certe Saul et ipse in praelio constitutus, manifeste munus istud indixit: Maledictus homo qui ederit panem ad vesperam usque dum ulciscur de inimico meo; et non gustavit totus populus ejus, et tota terra non prandebat. Tantam autem Deus praestitit auctoritatem edicto stationis illius, ut Jonathan filius Saulis, quanquam ignarus jejunationis in serum definitae gustum mellis admiserat, et sorte mox de delicto sit traductus, et vix per precem populi periculo exemptus, gulae enim, licet simplicis, reus fuerat. Sed et Daniel, anno primo regis Darii, cum jejunans in sacco et cinere exomologesin Deo ageret, et adhuc, inquit, loquente me in oratione, ecce vir quem videram in somnis initio, velociter volans adpropinquavit mihi quasi hora vespertini sacrificii. Haec erit statio sera, quae ad vesperam jejunans, pinguiorem orationem Deo immolat.
pass_a_gloss: They know our fasts, as unworthy; and some indeed, even established in the evening, they blame by the name of novelty, saying that this service also is to be performed by choice, and not to be extended beyond the ninth hour, according to their custom. But what pertains to the question of prohibition, I will respond once for all causes. Now, to the specific article of this kind, I speak about the manner of time, first to be demanded from them, whence they prescribe this new form for dismissing fasts. If, because Peter, and those with him, are read to have entered the temple for prayer at the ninth hour, who will prove to me that they performed a fast on that day, so that the ninth hour may be interpreted as the conclusion and ending of the fast? But you will more easily find Peter, for the sake of taking food, to have ascended to the upper rooms to pray at the sixth hour, so that the sixth day may be ended with this service, which seemed to be concluded after prayer. Furthermore, when in the same commentary of Luke, the third hour of prayer is shown, under which, having been initiated by the Holy Spirit, they were considered as drunkards; and the sixth, at which Peter ascended to the upper rooms; and the ninth, at which they entered the temple, why do we not understand that, with plain indifference, it is always and everywhere and at every time to pray, yet these three hours, as more notable in human affairs, which distribute the day, which distinguish businesses, which publicly resound, so also were more solemn in divine prayers? This is also suggested by the argument of Daniel, who prays three times a day, certainly through an exception of some hours, not others, however, than the more notable ones, from then on, the Apostolic, the third, the sixth, the ninth. Hence, I will also say that Peter, from an old custom, observed the ninth hour, praying at the third hour with the service of the highest prayer. But these things are on account of those who think they act according to Peter's form, which they do not know; not as if we reject the ninth hour, to which we also greatly observe the fourth of the Sabbath and the sixth; but because we ought to bring forth a worthy reason for those things which are observed from tradition, as much as they lack the authority of Scripture, until they are confirmed or corrected by some heavenly charisma. And if you are ignorant of anything, the Lord will reveal it to you. Therefore, having set aside the confirmator of all these things, the Paraclete, the leader of all truth, I ask whether a more unworthy reason is brought forth for observing the ninth hour, so that the same reason may be assigned to Peter, if he then performed a fast. For it comes from the departure of the Lord, which, although it ought to be commemorated always without difference of hours, we are more closely bound to it at that time, according to the very word of fasting; for even the soldiers are never unmindful of the sacrament, and more obedient to fasts. Therefore, the pressure is to be celebrated until that hour, in which, from the sixth hour, the darkened world, with the Lord dead, performed a mournful service, so that we also may return to joy, when the world also received light. If this savors more of Christian religion, while it celebrates the glory of Christ, I can equally establish the state of a late fast from the same order of things, so that we may fast until the evening, expecting the time of the Lord's burial, when Joseph requested and deposited the body. From then on, it is also irreligious to refresh the flesh of servants before that of the Lord. But I have permitted this from the provocation of arguments, conjectures to conjectures, and yet I think I have replied to the faithful, replying. Let us see if anything of this kind is also supported by the ancient things. In Exodus, the attire of Moses against Amalech, persevering in prayers until the evening, was it not a late fast? Do we think that Jesus, fighting the Amorites, ate on that day, on which he commanded a fast to the very elements? The sun stood still in Gabaon, and the moon in Aialon; the sun stood still and the moon by instruction, until the people were avenged of their enemies; and the sun stood in the middle of the sky, and did not hasten to its setting, and until the end of one day. There was not such a day before or afterwards, so prolonged; so that, as it is said, God heard the man, equal to the sun, persisting so long in the service, even a late and longer fast. Certainly, Saul, established in battle, clearly imposed this service: Cursed is the man who eats bread until the evening, until I am avenged of my enemy; and all his people did not taste, and all the land did not eat. God bestowed such authority on the edict of that fast, that Jonathan, the son of Saul, although ignorant of the fast defined until the evening, had taken a taste of honey, and soon was handed over to punishment for the fault, and was barely exempted from danger by the prayer of the people, for he was guilty of gluttony, although simple. But also Daniel, in the first year of King Darius, when, fasting in sackcloth and ashes, he made confession to God, and, while still speaking in prayer, behold, the man whom I saw in dreams at the beginning, quickly flying, approached me, like the hour of the evening sacrifice. This will be the late fast, which, fasting until the evening, offers a fuller prayer to God.

pass_b_english: They know our fasts as unworthy, and some even blame those established for the evening by calling them a novelty, claiming this service, too, must be performed by choice and not extended beyond the ninth hour—according to their own custom, of course. But on the question of prohibition I will answer once and for all. Now, on the specific point of timing: first let them explain where they get this new rule for dismissing fasts. If they appeal to the fact that Peter and his companions are recorded entering the temple for prayer at the ninth hour (Acts 3:1), who will prove they had actually fasted that day, so that the ninth hour could be taken as the fast's conclusion and end? You will more easily find Peter going up to the roof to pray at the sixth hour for the sake of taking food (Acts 10:9), so that the day's sixth hour might be finished by this service, which appeared to conclude after prayer. Moreover, when Luke's own account shows the third hour of prayer, when the Spirit-initiated were taken for drunkards; the sixth, when Peter went up to the roof; and the ninth, when they entered the temple—why do we not understand that, with complete indifference, we may always and everywhere and at every time pray, yet these three hours, as the more notable ones in human affairs—the hours that divide the day, distinguish business, and publicly resound—were therefore also the more solemn for divine prayers? Daniel's practice of praying three times daily supports this: he certainly excepted certain hours, and no others than the notable ones, which became the Apostolic hours of the third, sixth, and ninth (Daniel 6:10). Hence I say Peter observed the ninth hour out of an older custom, having prayed at the third hour with the service of the highest prayer. I say this for those who think they follow Peter's form but do not know it—not that we reject the ninth hour, to which we also observe the fourth day of the week and the sixth extensively; but because we must supply a worthy reason for what is kept by tradition precisely to the degree it lacks Scriptural authority, until it is confirmed or corrected by some heavenly charism. As the Lord says, "If you are ignorant of anything, the Lord will reveal it to you." So, setting aside the Paraclete, the confirmer of all these things and guide into all truth, I ask whether a more unworthy reason is offered for keeping the ninth hour, such that the same reason would have to be assigned to Peter if he indeed fasted then. For the ninth hour derives from the Lord's departure, which ought always to be commemorated without distinction of hours, yet we are more closely bound to it at that hour by the very word 'station': soldiers never forget their oath, and they are more obedient to their posts. Therefore the fast must be kept until that hour when, from the sixth hour onward, the darkened world performed a mournful service with the Lord dead, so that we too may return to joy when the world received its light. If this better suits Christian religion by celebrating Christ's glory, I can equally fix the rule for a late fast from the same sequence: we fast until evening, awaiting the hour of the Lord's burial, when Joseph requested and laid the body in the tomb. It becomes irreligious to refresh the flesh of servants before the Lord's. I have allowed this argument only under provocation—conjecture against conjecture—yet I think I have answered the faithful more faithfully. Let us see if the ancient records also support anything like this. In Exodus, was not Moses' stance against Amalek, persevering in prayer until sunset, a late fast (Exodus 17:11)? Do we think Joshua ate on the day he commanded the very elements to stand still for a fast while fighting the Amorites? The sun stood still at Gibeon and the moon at Aijalon; the sun stood still in mid-heaven and did not hasten to set for a whole day; there was no day like it before or since, so prolonged, that God might hear the man, equal to the sun, persisting so long in the service—a late and longer fast (Joshua 10:12-14). Saul, too, established in battle, explicitly imposed this service: "Cursed is the man who eats bread until evening, until I am avenged on my enemy"; none of his people tasted food, and all the land fasted (1 Samuel 14:24). God gave such authority to that fast's edict that Jonathan, Saul's son, though ignorant of the fast defined until evening, tasted honey and was handed over by lot for the offense, barely escaping death through the people's prayer—guilty of gluttony, though innocent (1 Samuel 14:24). And Daniel, in the first year of King Darius, fasting in sackcloth and ashes while making confession to God, said: "While I was still speaking in prayer, behold, the man I had seen in the vision at the first flew swiftly and touched me at the time of the evening sacrifice" (Daniel 9:3). This is the late fast: fasting until evening, it offers a fuller prayer to God.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text, including the complex theological arguments regarding the timing of fasts and the various biblical precedents. All scripture citations in Pass B (Acts 3:1, Acts 10:9, Daniel 6:10, Exodus 17:11, Joshua 10:12-14, 1 Samuel 14:24, Daniel 9:3) correctly identify the passages alluded to in the Latin. The distinction between 'station' (fast) and 'stationes' (fasts/fasting practices) is maintained. The translation of 'gulae, licet simplicis, reus fuerat' as 'guilty of gluttony, though innocent' is a valid interpretation of the context of Jonathan's unintentional transgression.
